claims.claim: Israel arrived in the wilderness of Sinai in the third month after the exodus, "the same day" (Ex 19:1–2).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:1–2, read in full.

claims.claim: Jubilees 1 dates the arrival to the sixteenth day of the third month (Jub 1:1).
claims.evidence: Charles, Jubilees 1:1, read in full. The Exodus text gives no day; the 16th is a Second Temple tradition.

claims.claim: Israel camped in the desert before the mount, having departed from Rephidim (Ex 19:2).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:2, read in full.

claims.claim: The giving of the law falls on the fiftieth day after the Passover (45 days from the departure plus the three days of preparation).
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 19:1 (45 days); Augustine, CD XVI.43 (fiftieth day; the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day). A traditional calculation, not stated in Ex 19:1.

claims.claim: Moses went up unto God, and the LORD called unto him out of the mountain (Ex 19:3).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:3, read in full.

claims.claim: God recited what he had done: "Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself" (Ex 19:4).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:4, read in full.

claims.claim: The covenant offer is conditional: "if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people" (Ex 19:5).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:5, read in full; BDB H1285 *bĕrît* (a divine constitution "with promises on condition of obedience").

claims.claim: *Sĕgullâ* (H5459) means "valued property, peculiar treasure," always of Israel, first occurring at Ex 19:5.
claims.evidence: BDB H5459, read in this session; LXX *laos periousios* (Tit 2:14; 1 Pet 2:9).

claims.claim: "Ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation" (Ex 19:6); BDB glosses the phrase as "priests and kings at once in their relation to the nations."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:6; BDB H3548 *kōhēn* sense 1, read in this session.

claims.claim: The people answered together, "All that the LORD hath spoken we will do" (Ex 19:8).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:8, read in full.

claims.claim: JFB reads the people's unanimous acceptance as showing self-confidence.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 19:8. A commentary reading, not a textual fact.

claims.claim: The people were sanctified for two days, washing their clothes, to be ready against the third day (Ex 19:10–11, 14–15).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:10–11, 14–15, read in full.

claims.claim: Bounds were set about the mount, with a death penalty for touching it — "whosoever toucheth the mount shall be surely put to death" (Ex 19:12–13).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:12–13, read in full.

claims.claim: The "priests" of Ex 19:22, 24 are a pre-Aaronic priesthood; BDB classes them with chieftains exercising priestly functions (cf. Jethro, Ex 2:16; 3:1).
claims.evidence: BDB H3548 *kōhēn* sense 1, read in this session; JFB on Ex 24:5 (the "young men" as priests, "probably the oldest sons").

claims.claim: Moses commanded the people, "come not at your wives" (Ex 19:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:15, read in full.

claims.claim: The abstinence of 19:15 is a purity requirement for the theophany (cf. the sanctification of vv. 10–11).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:10–15; Josephus, Ant. 3.5 (the people "abstained from their wives" for three days). The rationale is not stated in the text.

claims.claim: The LORD announced the theophany a day in advance, "that the people may hear when I speak with thee, and believe thee for ever" (Ex 19:9).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:9, read in full.

claims.claim: On the third day there were thunders, lightnings, a thick cloud, the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud, the mount smoking as a furnace, and the whole mount quaking greatly (Ex 19:16–19).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:16–19, read in full; Josephus, Ant. 3.5 (cloud, strong winds, rain, lightning, thunder).

claims.claim: The trumpet of Ex 19:16, 19 was miraculous, not human breath.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 19:16 ("the trumpet... was miraculous"). A commentary reading.

claims.claim: "Moses spake, and God answered him by a voice" (Ex 19:19).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:19, read in full.

claims.claim: The LORD came down upon Mount Sinai, on the top of the mount, and called Moses up (Ex 19:20).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:20, read in full.

claims.claim: Jebel Musa is the traditional identification of Mount Sinai, held since the fourth century CE.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 19 (Jebel Musa, now the traditional site; "It is not certain on which of these two they stood" — Jebel Musa or Es Suksafeh); the tradition that produced St. Catherine's Monastery (6th c.).

claims.claim: The location of Mount Sinai is not established; no identification is certain.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 19, read in full ("It is not certain on which of these two they stood" — Jebel Musa or Es Suksafeh); Hoffmeier, *Ancient Israel in Sinai* (2005), pp. 111–148 ("no one today can be certain of its location"); Kitchen, *On the Reliability of the Old Testament* (2003), p. 270 ("certainty is not attainable") — Hoffmeier/Kitchen quoted via search results only, see §12.4.

claims.claim: The LORD sent Moses down twice more with warnings that the people and the priests not break through to gaze, "lest the LORD break forth upon them" (Ex 19:21–24).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 19:21–24, read in full.

claims.claim: "And God spake all these words, saying" (Ex 20:1) — God spoke the Decalogue directly to the whole people.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:1, read in full; Josephus, Ant. 3.5 (the people heard the voice directly); Philo, De Decalogo §XXXIII (God promulgated the ten heads himself).

claims.claim: The preamble grounds the law in the exodus: "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage" (Ex 20:2).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:2, read in full; Calvin on Ex 20:1–2 (the preamble as "a general preface, whereby He prepares their minds for obedience").

claims.claim: The Decalogue is called "the words of the covenant, the ten words" (Ex 34:28; Dt 4:13).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 34:28; Dt 4:13; Clarke on Ex 20 (ʿăśeret had-dĕbārîm, "Ten Words").

claims.claim: The Decalogue exists in two versions, Ex 20 and Dt 5, agreeing in substance and differing in wording — above all in the Sabbath rationale (creation, Ex 20:11; deliverance, Dt 5:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:8–11; Dt 5:12–15; K&D on Ex 20 (catalogue of the variants); BDB H7676 *šabbāt* (the two rationales).

claims.claim: The Exodus text of the Decalogue is the original; the Deuteronomic variants are rhetorical and hortatory.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ex 20:1 (the variations "are rhetorical and hortatory," and "the text of Exodus [is] to be accepted as the original"). A scholarly judgment.

claims.claim: The first commandment forbids other gods "before me" (Ex 20:3); *ʿal-pānay* means "beyond Me / in addition to Me / by the side of Me" (K&D), not "in my presence" alone.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:3; K&D on Ex 20:3 (LXX *plēn emou*); Calvin on Ex 20:3 ("before my face" = over against, no companions).

claims.claim: The second commandment forbids any graven image or likeness, and any bowing down to or serving them (Ex 20:4–6).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:4–6, read in full; Calvin on Ex 20:4 (worship must be spiritual, corresponding to God's nature).

claims.claim: The threat and the promise of Ex 20:5–6 — visiting iniquity to the third and fourth generation, showing mercy unto thousands — are stated as part of the second commandment.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:5–6, read in full.

claims.claim: Clarke reads "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children" as national judgments, with children walking in their fathers' steps (Ezek 18).
claims.evidence: Clarke on Ex 20:5. A commentary reading, with Ezek 18 as the control.

claims.claim: The third commandment forbids taking the LORD's name in vain (Ex 20:7).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:7, read in full; Philo, De Decalogo §§XIV–XVII (the second commandment follows the first).

claims.claim: The fourth commandment is "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy," grounded in the six days of creation and God's rest on the seventh (Ex 20:8–11).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:8–11, read in full; BDB H7676 *šabbāt* ("P gives as basis God's resting Ex 20:11; 31:17").

claims.claim: The Sabbath is the most ancient institution (Gen 2:2), and "Remember" implies it was already known before Sinai.
claims.evidence: Clarke on Ex 20:8 ("Remember" implies the Sabbath was already known; Gen 2:2). A commentary reading.

claims.claim: Three numberings of the Decalogue are in use: the Jewish (preamble as first, image commandment merged), the Philonian/Reformed (five and five), and the Augustinian (three and seven).
claims.evidence: K&D on Ex 20:1 (the three views catalogued); Josephus, Ant. 3.5.5 ("five upon each table"); Philo, De Decalogo §XXIV (the first five commandments as "the one and more divine table").

claims.claim: Scripture gives "neither distinct statements, nor definite hints" on the numbering of the commandments or the arrangement of the tables.
claims.evidence: K&D on Ex 20:1, read in this session.

claims.claim: The fifth commandment is "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee" (Ex 20:12).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:12, read in full; Clarke on Ex 20:12 (the first commandment with a promise, Eph 6:2).

claims.claim: "Thou shalt not kill" (Ex 20:13) uses *rāṣaḥ*, which denotes unlawful killing with premeditation and is never used for judicial execution, holy war, or sacrificial slaughter.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:13; BDB H7523 *rāṣaḥ*, read in this session (the participle *rōṣēaḥ* is the unintentional manslayer, Dt 4:42; 19:3–6; Num 35).

claims.claim: The sixth through ninth commandments forbid adultery, stealing, false witness, and coveting (Ex 20:14–17).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:14–17, read in full.

claims.claim: The LXX order of the second table is adultery, steal, murder (NETS Ex 20:13–15), differing from the MT's murder, adultery, steal.
claims.evidence: NETS Exodus, Ex 20:13–15, read in full.

claims.claim: The tenth commandment forbids coveting the neighbour's house, wife, servants, ox, ass, "nor any thing that is thy neighbour's" (Ex 20:17).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:17, read in full; Clarke on Ex 20:17 (covet = desire to possess as property).

claims.claim: The people, seeing the thunderings, lightnings, trumpet, and smoking mountain, stood afar off and asked Moses to mediate: "Speak thou with us, and we will hear: but let not God speak with us, lest we die" (Ex 20:18–19).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:18–19, read in full; Dt 5:23–27 (the same request).

claims.claim: Moses drew near "unto the thick darkness where God was" (Ex 20:21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:21, read in full.

claims.claim: The altar law: an altar of earth; if of stone, not hewn stone; no steps, "that thy nakedness be not discovered thereon" (Ex 20:24–26).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 20:24–26, read in full.

claims.claim: JFB reads the prohibition of hewn stone as guarding against carved figures leading to superstition, and the prohibition of steps as a matter of decency.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 20:25–26. A commentary reading.

claims.claim: "Now these are the judgments which thou shalt set before them" (Ex 21:1) — the Book of the Covenant is a series of *mišpāṭîm*, judicial decisions, predominantly in casuistic ("if... then...") form.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:1; BDB H4941 *mišpāṭ* sense 4 ("plural of series of decisions Ex 21:1; 24:3 (JE)").

claims.claim: The Hebrew servant serves six years and goes out free in the seventh (Ex 21:2).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:2, read in full.

claims.claim: The servant who chooses to remain is brought before *ʾĕlōhîm*, his ear bored with an awl, and he serves for ever (Ex 21:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:6, read in full.

claims.claim: *ʾĔlōhîm* in Ex 21:6 and 22:8–9 is "judges" (the tribunal before which the case is brought); NETS renders it "tribunal of God" / "before God."
claims.evidence: NETS Exodus 21:6; 22:8–9, read in full; BDB H430 (not consulted in this session — see "Limitations"). The reading is live in the commentaries (JFB, K&D) and is not settled by the text alone.

claims.claim: The maidservant's protections (Ex 21:7–11): she is not to go out as the menservants do; if she please not her master, she is to be redeemed; she must not be sold to a strange nation; her food, raiment, and duty of marriage must not be diminished.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:7–11, read in full.

claims.claim: The capital offences of Ex 21:12–17 are murder, striking a parent, cursing a parent, and man-stealing.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:12–17, read in full.

claims.claim: The brawl law (Ex 21:18–19): the striker pays for the loss of time and for the healing.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:18–19, read in full; LH §206 (quarrel wound — oath and pay the physicians) as a parallel.

claims.claim: The beaten-servant law (Ex 21:20–21): a master who beats his servant to death "shall be surely punished," but if the servant survives a day or two, "he shall not be punished: for he is his money."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:20–21, read in full.

claims.claim: The ethical reading of Ex 21:20–21 — whether the law limits a master's power or licenses it — is disputed, and the "he is his money" clause is the ancient rationale, not an endorsement.
claims.evidence: The text as read; the difficulty is recorded in §8.8 and flagged for Yonatan's editorial judgment. No commentary read in this session settles it.

claims.claim: The pregnant-woman case (Ex 21:22–25): if no mischief follow, a fine as the judges determine; if mischief follow, "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:22–25, read in full; LH §§209–214 as the parallel case.

claims.claim: Lex talionis is a civil rule for magistrates, not a licence for private revenge.
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 21:24 ("the law... was a civil law for magistrates, not private revenge"). A commentary reading, consistent with the casuistic form.

claims.claim: The Talmudic reading of lex talionis (b. Bava Kamma 83b) is monetary compensation, not literal retaliation.
claims.evidence: Bava Kamma 83b — **not read directly** (see §12.4). Cited as a traditional reading, not as a verified source.

claims.claim: The goring-ox law (Ex 21:28–36): the ox is stoned and its flesh not eaten; if the ox was known to push and the owner did not keep it in, the owner dies or pays a ransom; the owner of a slave killed by the ox pays thirty shekels.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:28–36, read in full; LH §§250–252 as the parallel case.

claims.claim: The goring-ox parallel with LH §§250–252 is a shared case with different penalties: LH imposes a money fine (half a mina for a free-born man, one-third for a slave); Ex 21 requires the ox to be stoned and the owner to die or pay a ransom.
claims.evidence: LH §§250–252 (Avalon text, read in full); KJV Ex 21:28–32. The comparison is a scholarly judgment.

claims.claim: The thirty shekels of Ex 21:32 is the price of the slave; NETS renders it "thirty didrachmas."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 21:32; NETS Exodus 21:32, read in full.

claims.claim: Theft and restitution (Ex 22:1–4): five oxen for an ox, four sheep for a sheep, double for the thing found alive; the thief caught breaking in may be smitten, but not after sunrise.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 22:1–4, read in full.

claims.claim: The multiple-restitution principle of Ex 22:1–4 parallels LH §8 (thirtyfold for the god's or the court's property, tenfold for a freed man's), with different multipliers and no death penalty for theft in Exodus.
claims.evidence: LH §8 (Avalon text, read in full); KJV Ex 22:1–4. The comparison is a scholarly judgment.

claims.claim: The deposit and trust laws (Ex 22:7–13): the keeper of money or goods, the thief found or not found, the animal torn by beasts, the borrowed animal.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 22:7–13, read in full.

claims.claim: The stranger, the widow, and the fatherless are protected: "ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child" (Ex 22:21–24).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 22:21–24, read in full.

claims.claim: Usury is forbidden to the poor, and a neighbour's raiment taken in pledge must be returned by sunset, "for that is his covering only" (Ex 22:25–27).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 22:25–27, read in full.

claims.claim: "Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people" (Ex 22:28) — whether *ʾĕlōhîm* here means "gods," "God," or "judges" is not settled.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 22:28; NETS Exodus 22:28 ("You shall not revile gods"); BDB H430 not consulted in this session. The New Testament cites the verse as a prohibition on reviling a ruler (Acts 23:5 — see §11, conn-co-025).

claims.claim: The justice laws (Ex 23:1–9): no false report, no following a multitude to do evil, no perverting the judgment of the poor, no bribes, no oppressing the stranger.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 23:1–9, read in full.

claims.claim: The Sabbath year (Ex 23:10–11): six years of sowing, the seventh a rest for the land, that the poor may eat.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 23:10–11, read in full.

claims.claim: The three feasts (Ex 23:14–19): unleavened bread, harvest (firstfruits), and ingathering at the year's end; "Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 23:14–19, read in full.

claims.claim: The rationale of "Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk" (Ex 23:19) is not stated in the text; the Canaanite-cultic explanation is a modern proposal, not an established fact.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 23:19. No commentary read in this session settles the rationale; the Canaanite explanation is recorded as a proposal.

claims.claim: The Angel epilogue (Ex 23:20–23): "Behold, I send an Angel before thee, to keep thee in the way... my name is in him" — the Angel's identity is not settled in the text.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 23:20–23, read in full. The Angel of the LORD (Ex 3:2) and a created angel are both live readings; the dossier does not decide.

claims.claim: The conditional vs eternal covenant distinction (Sinai as conditional; Abraham, the Sabbath, and the new covenant as unconditional/eternal) is a scholarly classification, not a claim about the text's wording.
claims.evidence: Bible Odyssey, "Covenant in the Hebrew Bible," read in full (the distinction and the *bĕrît ʿôlām* evidence); BDB H1285 *bĕrît* (the Sinai covenant "with promises on condition of obedience").

claims.claim: The ratification (Ex 24:3–8): Moses told the people all the words; the people answered, "All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient"; the book of the covenant was read; blood was sprinkled on the altar and on the people — "Behold the blood of the covenant."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 24:3–8, read in full; JFB on Ex 24 (the altar as God, the twelve pillars as the tribes, Moses as mediator).

claims.claim: The elders "saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness. And upon the nobles of the children of Israel he laid not his hand: also they saw God, and did eat and drink" (Ex 24:9–11).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 24:9–11, read in full; NETS Exodus 24:10–11 ("like something made from lapis lazuli brick"; "not even one of the chosen of Israel perished").

claims.claim: JFB reads the elders' vision Christologically: a faint adumbrated form of Christ's humanity (cf. Ezek 1:26).
claims.evidence: JFB on Ex 24:10. A commentary reading.

claims.claim: Moses was called to the mount for the tables of stone, "a law, and commandments which I have written" (Ex 24:12), and was in the mount forty days and forty nights (Ex 24:18).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 24:12, 18, read in full; Josephus, Ant. 3.5 (forty days, fasting, "having tasted nothing"); Dt 9:9.

claims.claim: There is no direct archaeological evidence for the Sinai theophany or the giving of the law.
claims.evidence: §6.2 — the negative fact, stated as such. No inscription, sanctuary, or artefact from Sinai in the second millennium BCE can be tied to Ex 19–24.

claims.claim: The Egyptian presence in Sinai (Serabit el-Khadim, the Hathor temple, the Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions) is the archaeological context for the narrative's setting, not evidence of the exodus or the theophany.
claims.evidence: §6.1 — Serabit el-Khadim (turquoise/copper mines; Hathor temple founded under Senusret I, c. 1971–1926 BCE); Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions (Petrie, 1904–05; c. 1850–1550 BCE).

claims.claim: The covenant of Ex 19–24 maps onto the six-element Hittite suzerainty-treaty form (preamble, historical prologue, stipulations, document clause, witnesses, blessings and curses).
claims.evidence: Mendenhall (1954) via Wallace (2007) and Lucas (*Themelios* 8.1, 1982) — **summaries only, see §12.4**; Bible Odyssey, "Tablets and Treaties in the Ancient Near East," read in full (the four-part form).

claims.claim: The Exodus date is disputed between the early date (c. 1446 BCE, 1 Kgs 6:1, 480 years) and the late date (c. 1270–1250 BCE, Ex 1:11, Pi-Ramesses); most scholars who accept a historical Exodus favour the late date.
claims.evidence: §7.2. The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) is the terminus ante quem. Neither position is established to the standard the standards require.

claims.claim: The volcanic reading of the theophany (a volcanic eruption as the natural cause of the thunder, smoke, and earthquake) is recorded in the literature and is not adopted by this dossier.
claims.evidence: §4.3, §7.4. The theophany is accompanied by a voice speaking words, a summoned mediator, and a moral law — none of which a volcano supplies.

claims.claim: The Hammurabi comparison as a whole: the Book of the Covenant shares cases and the *lex talionis* formula with Hammurabi's Code, and differs from it in grading, vicarious punishment, and social protection — JFB's "primitive usages... incorporated, with modifications and improvements."
claims.evidence: §5.2 (the section-by-section comparison); JFB on Ex 21:1. The comparison is a scholarly judgment.

claims.claim: The early date's textual anchor is 1 Kings 6:1 (480 years from the exodus to Solomon's fourth year, c. 966/967 BCE); the late date's textual anchor is Ex 1:11 (Pithom and Raamses = Pi-Ramesses, Ramesses II, c. 1279–1213 BCE).
claims.evidence: KJV 1 Kgs 6:1; Ex 1:11. The anchors are established as texts; the dates they imply are Debated (clm-co-082).

connections.note: The mountain of the arrival is Horeb, where Moses saw the burning bush.
"I bare you on eagles' wings" — the eagle imagery recurs in Moses' song.
*Sĕgullâ* — "a peculiar treasure" / "a peculiar people" (BDB H5459).
*Sĕgullâ* — "they shall be mine... in that day when I make up my jewels" (BDB H5459).
"A chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people" — the LXX's "royal priesthood" (NETS 19:6) taken up verbatim.
"Kings and priests unto God" — the kingdom of priests fulfilled.
"Ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest" — the theophany contrasted with the approachable mountain.
The Decalogue's parallel account, with the different Sabbath rationale (Dt 5:15).
The Sabbath's creation grounding — God rested on the seventh day.
"Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise" — Paul quotes the fifth commandment.
"Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill" — Jesus' exposition of the sixth commandment.
"Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery" — Jesus' exposition of the seventh.
"Ye have heard that it hath been said... Thou shalt not forswear thyself" — Jesus' exposition of the oath commandment.
"I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet" — Paul on the tenth commandment.
The people's fear and the request for Moses to mediate, in the parallel account.
The brazen serpent — an image made at God's command, set against the prohibition of images (cf. JFB, Clarke on Ex 20:4).
"The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" — the individual-responsibility control on the visiting of iniquity (cf. Clarke on Ex 20:5).
The Hebrew servant law restated, with the release and the provision for the freed servant.
The ear-boring rite restated ("thou shalt take an awl, and thrust it through his ear unto the door").
"Mine ears hast thou opened" — JFB cites Ps 40:6 on the ear-boring rite.
The homicide law developed — the cities of refuge and the distinction between murder and manslaughter.
"Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: but I say unto you, That ye resist not evil."
The thirty pieces of silver — the price of the slave (Ex 21:32) as the price of the betrayal.
The stranger, the widow, and the fatherless — the social-protection laws restated.
Paul quotes Ex 22:28 ("Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people") before the council.
The Sabbath year restated, with the Jubilee.

"Whereupon neither the first testament was dedicated without blood... This is the blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you" — the ratification as the type of the new covenant's dedication.
"Behold the blood of the covenant" — "this is my blood of the new testament."
The tables of stone, "written with the finger of God," given at the end of the forty days.
The forty days restated — Moses "did neither eat bread nor drink water" in the mount.
The new covenant — "I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel" — set against the conditional Sinai covenant (cf. §8.1).
The law "was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator" — Paul on the law's mediation (cf. K&D on Ex 20:1, on Acts 7:53; Gal 3:19; Heb 2:2).

date.label: No independently established date
date.note: The date of the Exodus is debated (early vs. late); pending research question R1. Any future date assignment must apply consistently across all seven Exodus categories. Chronology is narrative only.

review.author: Gnosis research draft (AI-assisted)
review.notes: Part 3 verification 2026-11-18 (dossier/verification-batch2-20261118.md; combined verification-all7-20261118.md): 85 claims (Established 58, Probable 11, Debated 8, Traditional 8); 32 accepted + 4 rejected connections, all 72 range endpoints live-verified against the Preview API 2026-11-18; Decalogue presented unnumbered (no numbering tradition privileged); Sinai location presented with both positions (traditional Jebel Musa and the Arabian/Midianite position), neither adopted; treaty-form comparison presented as a scholarly comparison, not as evidence of a date; Jubilees 1 16th-day dating presented as a labelled Second Temple tradition, not as the biblical date; Ex 21:20-21 stated as written with a brief contextual note (the "he is his money" clause is the ancient rationale, not an endorsement); second-hand labels preserved verbatim in evidence (clm-co-023 Sinai location, Debated; clm-co-059 Talmudic lex talionis, Traditional; clm-co-081 treaty form, Probable); source-hittite-treaties is NIV per EM decision (treaties not read directly); no editorialOverride.
review.reviewer: Stage 1 dossier editorial verification 2026-11-18 (Part 3); independent QA not yet requested (in-review draft)
